The resulting absolute path is persisted to the manifest record (line 37).
findings.impact: Whoever controls the job arguments writes a PDF-shaped file anywhere the worker process can write, creating intermediate directories on the way: cron drop-ins, systemd units, ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, a Rails initializer, or overwriting an existing file such as a certificate or the spool of another tenant's manifest.
findings.recommendation: Never accept a caller-supplied filename: derive it from manifest.reference and a sanitised suffix, or at minimum File.basename it and re-check that target.realdirpath.start_with?(SPOOL.realpath.to_s).

triage.reason: The enqueue site is not in this snapshot (the manifests controller referenced by config/routes.rb:11 is absent), so the ingress that supplies args['filename'] cannot be cited from code. The parameter is a job argument with a documented user-facing origin ('the printable load manifest a dispatcher asked for', line 6), which is why the status is probable rather than confirmed.
No containment mitigation exists to evaluate: there is no basename, no expand_path check and no allow-list on the path.
Deterministic once the argument is controlled; the Pathname semantics were executed to confirm rather than assumed.

scope.established_by: Executed the exact Pathname#join the worker performs against both an absolute and a dot-dot argument, and read the two FileUtils calls that surround it.
scope.narrowed_by: The sibling parameter args['page'] is coerced with to_i (line 17) before interpolation into offset, so the same method's other injectable-looking string is in fact safe; only filename is unconstrained.

findings.title: Webhook dispatcher posts to an arbitrary caller-supplied URL (SSRF)
findings.evidence: url is taken as the third job argument (line 14) and handed straight to Faraday.new(url: url) (line 21) with no scheme allow-list, no host or IP validation, no redirect policy and no DNS-rebinding protection — the only configuration is a timeout (lines 22-23). The class comment says the destination 'may be one of the org's registered endpoints or a one-shot callback the partner asked us to hit' (lines 5-6), so a partner-chosen destination is the intended design. The request carries the org's HMAC signature header (line 26) and the event body (line 28), and the response status is written back to the event record (lines 31-35), giving a read-back channel.
findings.impact: A partner points the callback at http://127.0.0.1/internal/queues (the unauthenticated Sidekiq console mounted by config/initializers/sidekiq.rb:34), at the cluster metadata service, or at any internal HTTP service, and the worker issues the POST from inside the trust zone. Because response.status is persisted on the event, the attacker gets an oracle for internal port and path scanning; retry: 8 (line 10) makes it repeatable.
findings.recommendation: Resolve the host and reject loopback, link-local, and RFC1918 targets before connecting; require https and an allow-list of registered endpoints; disable redirect following; and route outbound webhooks through an egress proxy.

triage.reason: The enqueue site that supplies `url` is not in this snapshot, so the ingress cannot be cited from code; the worker's own documentation names a partner-supplied callback as the source, which is why status is probable.
Not a hardening nicety: unrestricted outbound requests to a caller-named host is the flaw class itself, and this repository contains an unauthenticated internal HTTP target that makes it actionable.
The claim is forged internal requests, not resource exhaustion.

scope.established_by: Read the single outbound HTTP construction in the module and checked for any validation between the argument and the connection; there is none.
scope.narrowed_by: The signature header is computed over the body with the org's own secret (line 19), so the secret itself is not disclosed to the SSRF target; the exposure is the request and the status oracle.

findings.title: Redis connection string falls back to a hardcoded password
findings.evidence: REDIS_URL = ENV.fetch("SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL", "redis://:sidekiq@localhost:6379/1") (sidekiq.rb:7). The fallback embeds the literal password 'sidekiq' and is used by both the server and client configurations (lines 14 and 27) whenever the environment variable is absent.
findings.impact: The credential is published in source control and any deployment that misses the environment variable authenticates with it. Anyone who can reach that Redis can read and write the job queues, which — given the queue ingress findings above — means executing arbitrary InboundEventWorker and ManifestRenderWorker payloads.
findings.recommendation: Remove the default and fail fast when SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL is unset; source the credential from the secrets manager.

triage.reason: Reported under the intrinsic-flaw rule, which names hardcoded static secrets explicitly.
It is a credential in source, not a missing header or an unauthenticated test helper.
Rule 13's exception exempts intrinsic flaws from trust-boundary tracing.

scope.established_by: Single definition; both configure blocks (lines 14, 27) read the same constant.
scope.narrowed_by: Only takes effect when SIDEKIQ_REDIS_URL is unset, and the host component is localhost, so the practical exposure depends on the deployment; hence low/probable.

findings.title: Profiles are self-writable and carry the role and org membership every rule depends on
findings.evidence: allow write: if request.auth.uid == uid (firestore.rules:31) lets any signed-in user write their own profile document with no field restrictions. That same document is the sole input to every authorization decision in the ruleset: profile() reads it (line 11), role() returns profile().role (line 15) and memberOf(orgId) tests `orgId in profile().orgs` (line 19). Those helpers gate org read (line 42), org write plus admin (line 43), the recursive org subtree (line 46) and the audit trail read (line 52). The client writes the document itself at first sign-in with a client-chosen orgId (web/src/auth.js:24-31), confirming the field is under client control by design.
findings.impact: Any account — including one created by self-service registration (auth.js:35-39) — patches its own profile to {role: 'admin', orgs: ['<any org id>']} and thereby obtains read and write over every organisation's documents and read over the audit trail. There is no server-side validation anywhere to contradict it; custom claims are not used.
findings.recommendation: Deny client writes to role and orgs: allow update only when request.resource.data.role == resource.data.role && request.resource.data.orgs == resource.data.orgs (or restrict the writable field set with hasOnly), and move role/membership assignment into an Admin-SDK function or custom claims.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: the Firestore client SDK write at web/src/auth.js:31 (setDoc on profiles/{uid}); the attacker is the authenticated writer of the very document the rules read.
No hypothetical caller is needed — the rules file both grants the write and consumes the written fields.
This is the authorization model itself, not a defence-in-depth extra.

scope.established_by: Walked every rule expression in the file and collected the ones whose truth depends on profile() — role() and memberOf() — then listed each allow clause that calls them.
scope.narrowed_by: The /catalog and /audits collections have `allow write: if false` (lines 25, 53), so this escalation grants reads there rather than writes; audits remain writable only through the Admin SDK (which is separately abusable via the seal endpoint, reported below).

findings.title: Recursive org wildcard grants every member full write over every other member's notes
findings.evidence: The nested `match /{document=**} { allow read, write: if memberOf(orgId); }` (lines 45-47) applies to every descendant of an org document. The web client stores notes at orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId} (web/src/notes.js:19, and the same path is used by functions/index.js:52 and :94), so notes fall entirely under this grant. The per-note ownership rules at lines 35-39 — which require resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid for read, update and delete — sit on the top-level /notes/{noteId} collection, which nothing in this repository writes to. Firestore evaluates allow rules as a union across matching paths, so the wildcard cannot be narrowed by the more specific block even if the paths did coincide.
findings.impact: Every member of an org can read, rewrite and delete any inspector's field notes, and can write any other subcollection under the org (members, settings, attachments metadata) regardless of role — the `role() == 'admin'` requirement on line 43 protects only the org document itself, not its subtree. Combined with the self-writable profile above, membership is self-granted, so this is reachable by any account.
findings.recommendation: Delete the recursive wildcard and write explicit rules per subcollection: for orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}, require memberOf(orgId) for read and resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid for update and delete; gate orgs/{orgId}/members on role() == 'admin'.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: web/src/notes.js:45 and :52 (updateDoc/deleteDoc issued by the client SDK directly against orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}); the client is the untrusted writer and the rules are the only check.
Verified that the collection path the client uses (notes.js:19) is the one the wildcard covers, and that the ownership block at line 35 matches a different, unused path.
Not an invented bypass of a working control: the ownership control is real but is written for a collection this application does not use.

scope.established_by: Collected every Firestore path literal used by the web client and the functions, then matched each against the rule blocks to see which block actually governs it.
scope.narrowed_by: Scoped to descendants of /orgs/{orgId}; /profiles, /catalog and /audits are governed by their own top-level blocks and are unaffected by this rule.

findings.title: Storage update rule allows any authenticated user to overwrite any note attachment
findings.evidence: Within the same match block, read (line 12), create (lines 14-17) and delete (line 22) all require noteOwner() == request.auth.uid, and create additionally caps size at 15 MB and restricts contentType to image/* or application/pdf. update requires only request.auth != null (line 20) — no owner check, no size cap, no content-type check. The comment attributes this to re-uploads after rotate/crop (line 19).
findings.impact: Any signed-in user overwrites any attachment in any org's notes with content of any type and any size: evidence photos on inspection records are replaceable (integrity of the field record is the product), storage cost is unbounded, and because contentType is unconstrained an attacker can serve text/html from the storage download URL that notes.js:63 writes back into the note document as lastAttachment.
findings.recommendation: Give update the same predicate as create: noteOwner() == request.auth.uid together with the size and contentType constraints.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: web/src/notes.js:61 uploadBytes against orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}/{file.name} — a client-issued Storage write where these rules are the only authorization.
Verified that the three sibling verbs in the same block do carry the owner predicate, so the omission on update is a real asymmetry and not a misreading.
Authentication exists; the missing piece is object-level authorization plus the two content constraints the same block applies on create.

scope.established_by: Compared the four verbs declared in the single match block for which predicates each carries.
scope.narrowed_by: Confined to the /orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId}/{fileName} prefix; /exports/{orgId}/{fileName} is `allow read, write: if false` (storage.rules:26) and is unaffected.

findings.title: adminApi Cloud Function has no authentication middleware
findings.evidence: The api express app installs both middlewares — api.use(corsMiddleware) then api.use(requireIdToken) (index.js:42-43). The adminApi app installs only the first: adminApi.use(corsMiddleware) at line 72, with no requireIdToken and no per-route guard on either handler. Both handlers use the Admin SDK, which bypasses Firestore rules entirely: GET /orgs/:orgId/members reads the whole members subcollection (lines 74-77) and POST /orgs/:orgId/seats writes the org document (lines 79-82). The app is exported as an onRequest function (line 111) and published at /admin/** by the hosting rewrite (firebase.json:7); v2 onRequest functions are invocable by allUsers unless an invoker restriction is set, and none is configured here.
findings.impact: Anonymous internet callers enumerate the full member roster (identities and whatever fields those documents carry) of any organisation whose id they can name or guess, and set that org's seatLimit at will. No token, no membership, no role.
findings.recommendation: adminApi.use(requireIdToken) plus an explicit admin-role check against the caller's profile or custom claims, and restrict the function's invoker to authenticated principals.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: the HTTP request itself — req.params.orgId at index.js:75 and :80 and req.body.seatLimit at line 80 are read from an unauthenticated request.
Not 'missing authentication on a local-only test function': adminApi is exported at line 111 and routed publicly by firebase.json:7.
Path traced rather than assumed: the hosting rewrite confirms this express app is served on the production domain.

scope.established_by: Diffed the middleware chains of the two express apps declared in the same file and confirmed neither adminApi route attaches a guard of its own.
scope.narrowed_by: The `api` app at lines 41-43 DOES install requireIdToken and is not part of this finding; the exposure is the second express app and its two routes only.

findings.title: exportOrgNotes callable performs no authentication or membership check
findings.evidence: The onCall handler validates only that request.data.orgId is a non-empty string (lines 89-92). It never reads request.auth, and it never checks membership the way the sibling REST route does — api.get('/notes/recent') loads the caller's profile and returns 403 unless orgId is in profile.orgs (index.js:47-50). The export then reads up to 5000 documents from orgs/{orgId}/notes with the Admin SDK, which bypasses Firestore rules, and returns id, ownerId, status, title and body as CSV (lines 94-100). The docstring acknowledges the elevated reach: 'Runs with the Admin SDK because the export spans every inspector's notes in the org' (lines 85-87).
findings.impact: Any caller who can name an org id — including an unauthenticated one, since callable functions accept anonymous invocations unless invoker restrictions are configured — downloads that org's entire field-note corpus, bodies included, in one call. This is the single highest-yield data exfiltration path in the application.
findings.recommendation: Reject when request.auth is undefined (throw HttpsError('unauthenticated')), then load the caller's profile and require orgId ∈ profile.orgs and an appropriate role — the exact check already written at lines 47-50.

triage.reason: Ingress cited: request.data.orgId at index.js:89 is caller-supplied and is the only input selecting which org's data is returned.
The missing check is in this handler, and the same file demonstrates the intended check twenty lines earlier.
Authorization on a bulk PII export is the primary control, not defence in depth.

scope.established_by: Compared every handler in the file for whether it consults request.auth / req.user and whether it verifies org membership; api.get('/notes/recent') does both, this callable does neither.
scope.narrowed_by: Limited to the notes subcollection of the named org and to 5000 documents per call (index.js:94); the call is repeatable but the ordering is fixed to updatedAt desc.

findings.title: Audit seal endpoint lets any caller forge or overwrite audit records for any org
findings.evidence: The audits collection is declared immutable to clients — allow write: if false (firestore.rules:53) with the comment 'Immutable trail written by the audit function with the Admin SDK' (line 50) — and readable only by admin or auditor roles (line 52). The seal handler writes it with the Admin SDK, which bypasses those rules, and applies no checks of its own: it does not verify that the caller belongs to the orgId it was handed (contrast index.js:47-50 in the same app, which does), and it composes the document id from two caller-supplied values — auditId = `${orgId}_${seq}` where both come from normalizeRequest of the request body (lines 60-61). The write is db.doc(...).set(payload) (line 62) with no merge option and no create-only precondition, so it replaces any existing document at that id.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user (requireIdToken is the only gate on this app) writes audit entries attributing seals to themselves for organisations they do not belong to, and — by replaying a known orgId/seq pair — overwrites existing audit records, destroying the immutable trail the rules file was written to protect. Because auditIds are a predictable {orgId}_{integer} pattern, enumeration is trivial.
findings.recommendation: Check org membership exactly as /notes/recent does, derive the audit id server-side (collection().add() or a server-generated sequence), and use .create() so an existing document cannot be replaced.

findings.title: Shared note view assigns the note body to innerHTML
findings.evidence: Every other value in the same function is written with textContent — the heading (line 30) and both fields of the metadata list (share.js:9-11) — but the body is assigned with article.innerHTML = note.body (line 39). note.body is stored verbatim by createNote (web/src/notes.js:33) with no sanitisation on write, and can be rewritten by updateNote (notes.js:44-49), which — under the recursive org rule at firestore.rules:46 — any org member may invoke against any note. The docstring frames the view as a link 'a supervisor sends to the site contact' (share.js:16-17).
findings.impact: An attacker who can write any note (per the rules findings above, any signed-in account) plants script in the body; it executes in the application origin for every recipient of the share link, including external site contacts, with access to the victim's Firebase session and therefore to their notes, profile document and any org data their profile grants.
findings.recommendation: Render the body as text (textContent) or sanitise it with a vetted HTML sanitiser and a strict allow-list before assignment; if rich text is required, store structured content rather than raw HTML.
